description_full: Alcoa Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the bauxite mining, alumina refining, aluminum production, and energy generation business in Australia, Brazil, Canada, Iceland, Norway, Spain, the United States, and internationally. The company operates through two segments: Alumina and Aluminum. It operates bauxite and other aluminous ores mining and processes bauxite into alumina for sale to aluminum smelter customers and customers who process it into industrial chemical products through supply contracts to third parties, as well as aluminum smelting and casting businesses. The company also offers aluminium powder and scrap and primary aluminum in the form of commodity grade ingot and value-add ingot to customers that produce products for transportation, building and construction, packaging, wire, and other industrial markets. In addition, it provides energy that generates and sells electricity in the wholesale market to traders, large industrial consumers, distribution companies, and other generation companies. The company was formerly known as Alcoa Upstream Corporation and changed its name to Alcoa Corporation in May 2016. The company was founded in 1886 and is headquartered in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

financial_summary: Alcoa Corporation is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $8.8B market cap on $12.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 11% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $567M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.02× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 7.7×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Free cash flow has compounded 69.1% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 4.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
